title: Mastering the Node.js Event Loop & Microtask Execution Order
summary: Explain and trace the exact order of execution among process.nextTick, Promise.then, setTimeout, setImmediate, and fs I/O callbacks.
problemStatement: In production, an Express API middleware is sporadically deferring high-priority cache lookups behind pending network I/O. Predict the exact execution order of the code snippet below and explain the mechanics of libuv event loop phases vs V8 microtask queues.
keyRequirements: Detail the distinction between the NextTick queue, Microtask queue (Promises), Timers phase, Poll (I/O) phase, and Check (setImmediate) phase.
Explain why process.nextTick starvation can lock the event loop.
Identify the exact console output order of the starter code.
Refactor the code to ensure a critical async operation does not starve I/O.
hints: Remember: process.nextTick is processed before Promise microtasks, and microtasks run immediately after the current operation finishes before moving to the next libuv phase.
Inside an I/O callback (poll phase), check phase (setImmediate) ALWAYS executes before timers phase (setTimeout) in the subsequent loop iteration.
rubric: Predicted the exact output sequence: 1, 10, 5, 4, 2, 3 (or 3, 2 depending on process startup), then 6, 9, 8, 7
Correctly explained that inside fs.readFile callback, setImmediate is guaranteed to run before setTimeout(0)
Explained how infinite recursive process.nextTick starves the I/O event loop while setImmediate does not

title: Sliding Window Log Rate Limiter using Redis Sorted Sets (ZSET)
summary: Implement a production-ready sliding window rate limiter in Node.js using Redis Sorted Sets to prevent API abuse.
problemStatement: Fixed-window rate limiters suffer from burst traffic at window boundaries (e.g. 100 reqs at 11:59 and 100 reqs at 12:00 = 200 reqs in 2 seconds). Build a sliding window rate limiter function `isAllowed(userId, limit, windowSeconds)` using Redis ZSETs where each request timestamp is stored as both score and member.
keyRequirements: Remove timestamps older than (currentTime - windowSeconds) using ZREMRANGEBYSCORE.
Count remaining elements in the set with ZCARD.
If count < limit, add the current timestamp with ZADD and refresh key TTL with EXPIRE.
Ensure the entire operation is atomic using a Redis Multi/Transaction or Lua script to avoid race conditions.
hints: Use Date.now() or high-resolution timestamp as the score in ZSET.
Wrap zremrangebyscore, zcard, zadd, and expire in redis.multi() or a Lua script so concurrent requests don't read stale counts.
rubric: Atomic execution via Redis transaction (MULTI/EXEC) or Lua script
Correctly evicts expired entries before checking ZCARD
Sets appropriate key TTL to avoid orphaned Redis memory
Returns remaining limit and retry/reset headers

title: Designing an Idempotent Payment & Order API
summary: Design and implement idempotency keys to ensure charging a card or placing an order is never executed twice during network retries.
problemStatement: Mobile clients and payment gateways often retry POST /api/orders on network drops or timeouts. If the original request actually succeeded on the server, the user could be charged twice. Design an Idempotency Middleware and database pattern.
keyRequirements: Inspect Idempotency-Key HTTP header from the client.
Acquire an atomic processing lock in Redis with SET key value NX EX 30.
If lock fails and status is 'processing', return HTTP 409 Conflict or 425 Too Early.
If key already has a cached completed response in MongoDB/Redis, return the exact cached response with an 'Idempotent-Replay: true' header.
If it is a new request, execute handler, persist the response body and status, and release the processing lock.
hints: Store both request hash (to detect payload tampering with the same key) and response body.
Handle server crash while status is 'processing' — TTL on the lock is critical!
rubric: Handled 3 distinct states: First request (process), Concurrent duplicate (wait/conflict), Completed duplicate (replay cached response)
Detected payload mismatch for reused idempotency keys
Guaranteed atomic lock acquisition via Redis SET NX EX

title: Database Indexing & The ESR (Equality, Sort, Range) Rule
summary: Optimize complex multi-predicate database queries using compound B-Tree indexes and the ESR rule.
problemStatement: A high-traffic e-commerce query searches for orders: `status = 'SHIPPED'` AND `userId = 123` AND `createdAt >= '2026-01-01'` ORDER BY `totalAmount DESC`. The current query is doing full collection scans causing high CPU load. Design the optimal compound index and explain why.
keyRequirements: Explain the ESR (Equality, Sort, Range) rule and why index order determines scan efficiency.
Compare index `(status, userId, totalAmount, createdAt)` vs `(createdAt, status, userId, totalAmount)`.
Explain index selectivity, covering indexes, and index prefix matching.
Write the exact Mongoose schema index or PostgreSQL CREATE INDEX statement.
hints: E (Equality fields first): status, userId
S (Sort fields next): totalAmount (avoids in-memory sorting)
R (Range fields last): createdAt (once a range operator is evaluated, subsequent index keys cannot be used for sorting)
rubric: Identified correct index order: { status: 1, userId: 1, totalAmount: -1, createdAt: 1 } (or userId first)
Explained that putting range fields before sort forces an expensive in-memory sort
Explained covering index concept (indexOnly: true in explain plan)

title: Debugging Node.js Memory Leaks & V8 Heap Profiling
summary: Identify common Node.js memory leak patterns (closures, event listeners, global caches) and how to diagnose them.
problemStatement: A microservice's memory continuously grows from 150MB to 1.8GB until it crashes with 'JavaScript heap out of memory'. Below are 3 code snippets. Identify which ones leak memory, why V8 garbage collection (Mark & Sweep) cannot collect them, and how to fix them.
keyRequirements: Analyze closures retaining outer scope variables.
Analyze unremoved EventEmitter / socket event listeners.
Analyze unbounded in-memory cache objects without eviction / LRU.
Demonstrate how to generate heap snapshots in Node.js using `v8.getHeapSnapshot()` or `--inspect`.
hints: In Snippet B: If req.on('close') is not removing the listener from globalEmitter, each HTTP request adds a permanent callback to the emitter!
In Snippet A: Without a max size or LRU/TTL, cache grows indefinitely. Redis or an lru-cache should be used.
rubric: Identified memory leak mechanics in all 3 snippets
Wrote cleanup logic for event emitters (`req.on('close', () => globalEmitter.removeListener(...))`
Explained generation of heap snapshot with `--max-old-space-size` and inspection in Chrome DevTools

title: Distributed Locking with Redis (Redlock Algorithm & Fencing Tokens)
summary: Implement a distributed lock in Redis with auto-expiry, unique owner identifiers, and safe atomic release via Lua.
problemStatement: Two background workers run concurrently and attempt to generate the monthly invoice for the same tenant. If both run simultaneously, duplicate invoices and charges occur. Build a distributed lock helper `withLock(lockKey, ttlMs, callback)`.
keyRequirements: Acquire lock using `SET key random_uuid NX PX ttlMs`.
Release lock safely using a Lua script that checks if the lock value matches the unique `random_uuid` before calling `DEL` (avoids deleting a lock acquired by another worker if TTL expired).
Explain the problem of GC pauses / network lags causing lock expiration while work is in progress.
Explain Martin Kleppmann's fencing token solution for distributed locks.
hints: Lua script for safe release: `if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end`
Fencing token: An auto-incrementing integer returned with each lock acquisition so the storage engine rejects writes with smaller tokens.
rubric: Used unique UUID for lock owner verification
Released lock exclusively via Lua script
Accurately explained fencing token counter mechanics

title: Secure OTP Generation, TTL Caching & Brute-Force Rate Limiting
summary: Design a secure, production-grade OTP generation and verification flow using Redis expiration and attempt throttling.
problemStatement: Build an authentication OTP service in Express + Redis. Users can request a 6-digit OTP sent to their email/phone. The OTP expires in 5 minutes. To prevent brute-force attacks, lock the account after 3 consecutive wrong attempts and rate-limit OTP generation to at most 1 request every 60 seconds.
keyRequirements: Generate cryptographically secure 6-digit OTP using `crypto.randomInt(100000, 999999)`.
Store OTP in Redis with `EX 300` (5 min TTL) hashed (e.g. SHA-256 or bcrypt) so plaintext OTP isn't exposed in Redis dumps.
Enforce cooldown: check `otp:cooldown:user` key with 60s TTL before allowing resend.
Track attempts: maintain `otp:attempts:user` key. On 3 wrong attempts, delete OTP and block for 15 minutes.
hints: Use crypto.timingSafeEqual when comparing hashes to prevent timing attacks.
Delete the OTP immediately after successful verification to prevent replay attacks.
rubric: Stored hashed OTP with TTL in Redis
Implemented 60-second generation cooldown
Tracked attempts and locked after 3 failures
Cleaned up keys after success or lockout

title: Streaming Massive Datasets in Node.js without High Memory Usage
summary: Process a 5GB CSV file or stream a large database export directly to HTTP response using Node.js Streams and backpressure handling.
problemStatement: An endpoint `/export/transactions.csv` crashes the server with Out-of-Memory when exporting 500,000 records. Refactor the endpoint to stream data from the database cursor directly into an HTTP response using Node.js stream pipelines, Transform streams, and proper backpressure.
keyRequirements: Explain the 4 types of Node.js streams (Readable, Writable, Transform, Duplex).
Explain backpressure: what happens when readable stream produces data faster than writable stream can consume.
Use `stream.pipeline` instead of `.pipe()` to ensure proper cleanup on client abort / network errors.
Transform database documents into CSV chunks on the fly.
hints: Using .pipe() does not automatically destroy streams when an error occurs, leading to memory/file descriptor leaks. Always use pipeline() from 'stream/promises' or 'stream'.
Use mongoose Query.cursor() or pg-query-stream to fetch rows in small chunks.
rubric: Used database cursor stream instead of loading all rows into RAM
Used pipeline() for robust error handling and stream teardown
Correctly implemented Transform stream to format CSV rows

title: Cache Invalidation Strategies: Cache-Aside vs Write-Through vs Write-Behind
summary: Deep dive into cache consistency, cache stampede (dogpiling), cache penetration, and cache avalanche solutions.
problemStatement: Your application has 10,000 requests per second reading product details. You must prevent 3 classic caching catastrophes: Cache Stampede (hot key expires and 5000 queries hit DB simultaneously), Cache Penetration (queries for non-existent IDs bypass cache), and Cache Avalanche (many keys expire at the same second).
keyRequirements: Implement Cache-Aside with probabilistic early expiration (XFetch) or mutex lock to solve Cache Stampede.
Solve Cache Penetration using Bloom Filters or caching empty results (null values) with short TTL.
Solve Cache Avalanche by adding jitter (randomized seconds) to key expiration.
Compare Delete-on-Update vs Update-on-Update for database consistency.
hints: Cache Avalanche fix: `const ttl = baseTTL + Math.floor(Math.random() * 300);`
Cache Stampede: Use a small Redis lock `SET lock:key token NX EX 5`. Only the winner queries the DB; losers sleep 50ms and retry cache.
rubric: Implemented mutex lock or early refresh on cache miss
Cached empty sentinel values for non-existent IDs with TTL
Applied jitter to TTLs to prevent synchronized expiration
Explained dual-write inconsistency risks

title: Designing a Webhook Delivery Engine with Exponential Backoff & DLQ
summary: Architect a reliable webhook delivery system that guarantees at-least-once delivery, signs payloads with HMAC, and isolates failing endpoints.
problemStatement: Your payment platform needs to dispatch webhooks (e.g. `payment.succeeded`) to external merchant servers. Merchant servers can be slow, crash, or return 500s. Design a resilient queue worker system with HMAC-SHA256 signatures, retry intervals (1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 24h), and a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ).
keyRequirements: Sign webhook body using `crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret)` and send signature in `X-Signature-SHA256` header.
Implement exponential backoff retry scheduling.
Move to Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) after 5 failed attempts.
Prevent slow merchant servers from clogging the queue (per-merchant concurrency limits or circuit breakers).
hints: Set an aggressive HTTP timeout (e.g. 5 seconds) on outgoing webhook calls so slow servers don't consume your worker threads.
Store timestamp in signature to allow merchants to prevent replay attacks.
rubric: HMAC-SHA256 signature generation and verification protocol
Calculated exponential backoff schedule with jitter
Isolated failed webhooks into DLQ for manual inspection or alert

title: Complex MongoDB Aggregation Pipelines: $facet, $lookup, and Performance
summary: Build multi-stage aggregation pipelines for faceted search, pagination, and correlated lookups without memory exhaustion.
problemStatement: Build an analytical query endpoint that returns: 1) Paginated search results of orders matching criteria, 2) Total matching count, 3) Breakdown of sales total grouped by product category, and 4) Top 5 buying users — all in a single database roundtrip using $facet.
keyRequirements: Use $match as the very first stage to leverage database indexes.
Use $facet to run multiple aggregation sub-pipelines simultaneously.
Avoid the 100MB RAM aggregation limit using allowDiskUse or optimized index-covered grouping.
Perform correlated $lookup with pipeline subqueries.
hints: Remember: $match and $sort at the start of pipeline can use indexes; after an $unwind or $group, indexes are no longer used for subsequent filtering.
$facet cannot use indexes directly inside its sub-pipelines, so filter globally first!
rubric: Placed $match at the very beginning to hit indexes
Structured $facet for parallel pagination metadata and aggregations
Demonstrated awareness of the 100MB BSON memory limit

title: Graceful Shutdown in Node.js (Zero-Downtime Deployments & Signal Trapping)
summary: Handle SIGTERM and SIGINT cleanly: stop accepting new requests, drain active connections, and close DB pools.
problemStatement: When Kubernetes deploys a new container pod or ECS terminates a task, it sends SIGTERM. If your app terminates immediately with process.exit(0), active customer requests are abruptly severed and database transactions remain uncommitted. Write a production-grade graceful shutdown coordinator.
keyRequirements: Intercept process.on('SIGTERM') and process.on('SIGINT').
Stop the HTTP server from accepting new connections via `server.close()`.
Wait for existing in-flight HTTP requests to complete (with a hard timeout fallback, e.g. 15s).
Close MongoDB connections, Redis clients, and background message queue workers cleanly.
Exit with process.exit(0) on clean exit, or process.exit(1) on forced timeout.
hints: In Node.js 18.2+, `server.closeIdleConnections()` can be called immediately to terminate keep-alive sockets that aren't handling an active request.
Make sure health check endpoints (/healthz) start returning 503 Service Unavailable immediately upon receiving SIGTERM so load balancers reroute traffic.
rubric: Trapped both SIGTERM and SIGINT
Closed HTTP server and set hard deadline timeout
Closed Mongoose and Redis connections cleanly
Handled forced exit on timeout

title: Redis Pub/Sub vs Redis Streams vs Consumer Groups
summary: Architect message-driven communication using Redis Streams (XADD, XREADGROUP, XACK) for persistent, fault-tolerant processing.
problemStatement: A team used Redis Pub/Sub for background video processing notifications. When a worker restarted or crashed, all messages published during the downtime were permanently lost because Redis Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget. Migrate the architecture to Redis Streams with Consumer Groups.
keyRequirements: Contrast Redis Pub/Sub (at-most-once, no persistence) with Redis Streams (at-least-once, log-based persistence).
Publish messages using `XADD mystream * payload data`.
Create a consumer group using `XGROUP CREATE`.
Read messages using `XREADGROUP GROUP mygroup worker1 COUNT 10 BLOCK 2000 STREAMS mystream >`.
Acknowledge processed messages with `XACK` and claim stalled messages using `XAUTOCLAIM`.
hints: Use `MKSTREAM` flag when creating the group so Redis creates the stream if it doesn't already exist.
Remember: The special ID '>' means 'give me messages never delivered to any consumer in this group'.
rubric: Correctly explained limitations of Pub/Sub vs Streams
Implemented consumer group polling with XREADGROUP
Included XACK for delivery acknowledgment and recovery of pending entries

title: SQL ACID Isolation Levels & Preventing Race Conditions
summary: Examine Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, Phantom Reads, and Serialization Anomalies across SQL isolation levels.
problemStatement: Two concurrent transactions attempt to book the last available seat on a flight. Under default READ COMMITTED isolation, both check `SELECT count(*) WHERE booked = false`, find 1 seat, and execute `INSERT INTO bookings`. Both receive confirmation! Demonstrate how to solve this using Optimistic Locking vs Pessimistic Locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE) vs SERIALIZABLE.
keyRequirements: Define the 4 standard SQL isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE.
Explain the phenomenon of Dirty Read, Non-Repeatable Read, and Phantom Read.
Write a Pessimistic Lock query using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.
Write an Optimistic Lock query using a version/timestamp column and compare trade-offs.
hints: Pessimistic locking is ideal for high-contention write scenarios where conflicts are frequent (e.g. ticket booking).
Optimistic locking is superior for read-heavy scenarios with low write contention because it avoids holding row locks.
rubric: Accurately defined all 4 isolation levels and anomaly types
Provided functional Pessimistic (FOR UPDATE) and Optimistic (version match) SQL examples
Compared performance and deadlock risks

title: Building an Async Concurrency Limiter (p-limit) from Scratch
summary: Implement a custom concurrency pool to execute 1,000 async tasks with at most N running concurrently.
problemStatement: `Promise.all(urls.map(fetch))` fires all 1,000 requests simultaneously, exhausting network sockets, triggering 429 Too Many Requests, and crashing external APIs. Without using third-party packages like `p-limit`, build a lightweight concurrency limiter `pLimit(concurrency)` from first principles.
keyRequirements: Accept a maximum concurrency limit `N` (e.g. 5).
Return a wrapper function `limit(fn)` that returns a Promise.
Enqueue tasks in an internal queue if active workers == N.
When an active task settles (resolves or rejects), immediately pull the next task from the queue and execute it.
Ensure all original rejection and resolution values propagate correctly.
hints: Define a next() helper: if activeCount < concurrency and queue has items, dequeue, activeCount++, execute, and on complete activeCount--, next().
Always attach .finally() or try/finally so activeCount decrements even on errors!
rubric: Guaranteed that no more than N promises run simultaneously
Handled rejections properly without breaking the queue
Maintained execution order and returned resolved values

title: Counting Billions of Unique Users with Redis HyperLogLog & Bitmaps
summary: Calculate Daily Active Users (DAU) and Monthly Active Users (MAU) using Redis HyperLogLog and Bitmaps with fixed memory.
problemStatement: Your service tracks 100 million daily active users. Storing user IDs in a Redis SET requires ~1.5GB of RAM per day. Switch to Redis HyperLogLog (PFADD, PFCOUNT, PFMERGE) for cardinality estimation with < 12KB memory and 0.81% error rate, or Bitmaps (SETBIT, BITCOUNT, BITOP) for exact user activity tracking.
keyRequirements: Use `PFADD dau:2026-09-20 userId` to register user visits.
Calculate DAU with `PFCOUNT dau:2026-09-20`.
Calculate weekly/monthly active users by merging logs with `PFMERGE mau:september dau:day1 dau:day2 ...`.
Compare HyperLogLog (probabilistic, fixed 12KB) vs Bitmap (exact, 1 bit per user ID) vs Set.
hints: HyperLogLog uses standard 12KB memory regardless of whether you have 100 or 100,000,000 items.
Bitmaps require auto-incrementing integer user IDs (e.g. user #5421 maps to bit index 5421).
rubric: Demonstrated usage of PFADD and PFCOUNT
Explained memory trade-off (12KB fixed size vs Set memory growth)
Used BITOP AND/OR to analyze recurring user retention

title: Designing a Multi-Channel Notification Service (Email, SMS, Push)
summary: Architect an enterprise notification service supporting priority queues, user preferences, rate limiting, and vendor fallbacks.
problemStatement: Design a notification platform capable of dispatching 10 million notifications daily across Email (SendGrid/SES), SMS (Twilio), and Push (FCM). The system must support user opt-outs, deduplication, priority channels (OTP/Security vs Marketing), and automatic failover to secondary vendors if primary vendor returns 5xx.
keyRequirements: Design message ingestion API with priority tiers (High: OTP/Alerts, Normal: Receipts, Low: Marketing).
User preference engine: Check if user unsubscribed or set 'Quiet Hours' (e.g. no push between 10pm-8am).
Per-user notification rate limiter (max 3 marketing emails per day).
Circuit breaker & vendor failover for external SMS/Email APIs.
hints: Use separate message queues for each priority tier so promotional email blasts never delay time-critical password reset OTPs.
Store idempotency key per notification to prevent duplicate SMS charges on retries.
rubric: Separated queues by priority to prevent starvation
Checked user preferences and quiet-hours timezone logic
Included circuit breaker / vendor fallback logic
Guaranteed deduplication via unique event hash

title: Scaling Databases: Sharding vs Partitioning vs Read Replicas
summary: Evaluate vertical vs horizontal scaling, primary-replica replication lag, and sharding strategies (Hash vs Range vs Geo).
problemStatement: Your PostgreSQL/MongoDB database has grown to 5TB and 30,000 queries per second. A single large instance can no longer sustain the write load and replication lag to read replicas is causing users to see stale data after updates. Architect a horizontal scaling and sharding strategy.
keyRequirements: Compare Read Replicas (read scaling) vs Sharding (write scaling).
Explain Replication Lag and how to ensure 'Read-Your-Own-Writes' consistency.
Choose a Shard Key for an e-commerce platform (e.g. userId vs orderId vs tenantId) and explain hot spotting / celebrity problem.
Explain how cross-shard joins and distributed transactions (2PC - Two-Phase Commit) are handled.
hints: Strategy 1 for Read-Your-Own-Writes: Route reads from the same user to the Primary DB for a few seconds following any write.
Strategy 2: Track Write LSN (Log Sequence Number) and only read from replicas that caught up to that LSN.
rubric: Distinguished read scaling (replicas) from write scaling (sharding)
Selected appropriate shard key and addressed data skew / re-sharding
Explained Read-Your-Own-Writes solutions (LSN / sticky session to primary)

title: Worker Threads & Clustering in Node.js for CPU-Intensive Tasks
summary: Offload CPU-intensive operations (image resizing, PDF generation, heavy cryptography) without blocking the Node.js event loop.
problemStatement: A single route `/generate-report` does a heavy 3-second cryptographic calculation. When 10 users hit it, all other API requests are blocked and time out because Node's single thread is monopolized. Compare and implement Node's `cluster` module vs `worker_threads`.
keyRequirements: Explain the difference between Node's Cluster module (multiple OS processes sharing a port) and Worker Threads (threads sharing memory via SharedArrayBuffer).
Spawn a worker thread using `worker_threads` to process CPU work.
Pass data to worker and receive results using `parentPort.postMessage()`.
Ensure thread pool reuse rather than creating new threads per HTTP request.
hints: Spawning a thread has memory and CPU overhead (approx 20-30ms). Use a worker pool (like piscina) in production.
For I/O tasks, worker threads do NOT add performance because libuv already handles async I/O in the threadpool!
rubric: Clear distinction between Cluster (processes) and Worker Threads (threads)
Correct implementation of Worker instance and message passing
Proper error handling when worker throws an unhandled exception

title: Token Bucket Rate Limiter with Atomic Redis Lua Scripts
summary: Implement the Token Bucket algorithm in Redis using a Lua script to support smooth burst handling with zero race conditions.
problemStatement: Unlike sliding window logs (which store every timestamp and consume high memory), Token Bucket allows bursts up to capacity `C` and refills tokens at rate `R` tokens per second using only 2 stored numbers: current tokens and last refill timestamp.
keyRequirements: Store `{ tokens, lastRefillTimestamp }` in a Redis Hash.
Write a Redis Lua script: calculate elapsed time, refill tokens proportionally up to bucket capacity, and decrement 1 token if available.
Execute the script via `redis.eval()` with atomic guarantees.
Return headers: `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `Retry-After`.
starterCode:
const tokenBucketLua = `
-- KEYS[1]: rate limiter key
-- ARGV[1]: capacity (max tokens)
-- ARGV[2]: refill rate (tokens per second)
-- ARGV[3]: current timestamp in seconds
-- ARGV[4]: requested tokens (default 1)

-- TODO: Write Lua script to refill and consume tokens
`;
hints: Tokens to add: `math.min(capacity, current_tokens + (elapsed * refill_rate))`
If `tokens >= requested`, decrement and return 1 (allowed), else return 0 (rejected).
rubric: Correct token refill math based on elapsed time
Lua script guarantees atomicity without Redis transactions or race conditions
Memory efficient: only stores 2 fields per user/IP
